set.text: When Amara and her cousin Joel planned a two-day hike across a dry valley, an old ranger gave them one warning: carry more water than you think you need. The land there is arid; it can go many weeks without a single drop of rain. Plants are sparse, mostly low bushes standing far apart, so there is almost no shade. The first climb was strenuous, and by noon both of them were breathing hard. Joel, who runs marathons, had more stamina, but even he slowed down. Late in the afternoon Amara pointed at a shining lake ahead. Joel laughed. It was a mirage, made by hot air bending the light. Without the ranger's advice, the trip could have been perilous. Instead, they finished tired, sunburned and proud, with one full bottle of water still in each pack.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sparse” mean?
qs.why: The next words explain it: low bushes “standing far apart,” so there is little shade. “Tall and thick” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mirage” mean?
options: something that looked like water but was not really there
a small lake fed by an underground spring
a real pond reflecting the sky
a dream Amara had while resting
a trick Joel played on Amara
a sign that rain was coming
qs.why: Joel laughs because the shining lake is a mirage, caused by hot air bending light; there was no real water. It was not a trick by Joel.

qs.q: What does the passage suggest made the trip end safely?
options: Joel's marathon training carried them both
They followed the ranger's advice and carried extra water
They found shade under tall trees
They drank from the lake they saw
qs.why: The passage says the trip could have been dangerous without the ranger's advice, and they still had a full bottle each at the end. The lake was a mirage, so they could not drink from it.

why: Correct option for 'sparse' was ungrammatical ('spread thinly far apart'); reworded.

set.text: When the venerable Hollis Library, open since 1790, cleaned out its attic, a volunteer named Grace Okafor found a small book wrapped in cloth. Inside was a handwritten treatise on beekeeping, page after page about hives, honey and the habits of queen bees. The spelling was archaic, full of words nobody has used for two hundred years, and the ink had faded to brown. It took Grace and two experts a month to decipher the hardest pages. Next came the question of provenance. Who had written it, and how had it reached the attic? A note in the back led them to a farming family that had given books to the library in the 1800s. The experts believe it is the only extant copy of the work, which makes it the most valuable book the library owns.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “provenance” mean?
options: where it came from and who had owned it
the main subject of the book
qs.why: The next questions explain it: who wrote it and how it reached the attic. Its value comes later and is a different idea.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “extant” mean?
qs.why: The experts think this is the only copy still in existence. “Lost long ago” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why is the book so valuable to the library?
options: It is the oldest book in the world
It was written by a famous scientist
It explains how to earn money from honey
It is believed to be the only copy of the work still in existence
qs.why: The last sentence links its value to being the only copy that still exists. Nothing says it is the oldest book in the world or by a famous author.

why: A 'thin book' contradicted 'treatise' (a long, detailed work) and 'page after page'; changed to 'small book'.

set.text: Few issues in Maple Falls have been as contentious as the plan to turn half of Riverside Field into a dog park. At last Tuesday's town meeting, dog owners filled one side of the room and youth soccer parents filled the other. Each group had a grievance: dog owners said they had nowhere to let pets run, while parents said their children already had too little space to play. Town leaders asked a retired judge, Eleanor Voss, to mediate. Everyone agreed she would be impartial, since she owns no dog and has no children on a team. Voss let each side speak for ten minutes. Then she proposed using a fenced corner of the field on weekday mornings only, when no games are played. One by one, speakers stood to concur. Before closing, Voss chose to reiterate the agreement so no one could later claim to have misunderstood it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mediate” mean?
options: decide who was right and punish the other side
help the two sides reach an agreement
qs.why: Voss listened to both sides and suggested a plan they could accept. A judge in court might decide who is right, but here she helped them agree.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “reiterate” mean?
options: say again to make it clear
qs.why: She repeated the agreement so no one could later say they misunderstood it. She did not change it.

qs.q: Why was Eleanor Voss chosen to lead the discussion?
options: She had no personal stake in either side
She had written the dog park plan
qs.why: People trusted her to be fair because she owns no dog and has no child on a team. Nothing says she owned the field, led the town, coached soccer or wrote the plan.

why: 'why' for the idea question wrongly claimed every wrong option would make Voss favor one side (e.g. being mayor would not); rewritten.

set.text: Six-year-old twins Ollie and Zara are known in their family as the most mischievous children on the block. Last Saturday they wanted the chocolate cookies cooling on the kitchen counter, so they came up with a ruse. Zara ran into the garden shouting that she had seen a deer. The commotion worked. Their father, Ben, rushed outside, and their grandmother followed with her phone, hoping for a photo. Ollie, meanwhile, climbed onto a chair and grabbed six cookies. He was so focused that he was oblivious to the family cat, which jumped onto the counter beside him and knocked the whole tray to the floor. Ben came back inside at the crash. He could barely restrain his laughter at the sight of Ollie, the cat and a floor covered in crumbs. He was angry only momentarily.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ruse” mean?
options: a clever trick to fool someone
qs.why: Zara's fake deer was a trick to get the adults out of the kitchen. An honest request is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “oblivious” mean?
qs.why: Ollie was so focused on the cookies that he did not notice the cat. “Watching closely” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did Zara shout that she had seen a deer?
options: So her grandmother would take her photo
To get the adults outside so Ollie could take cookies
To warn her father about danger
qs.why: The shout was part of the twins' trick to reach the cookies. The grandmother wanted a photo of the deer, not of Zara.

why: Title 'Six Cookies Short' did not match the text (Ollie grabbed four cookies); made it six.

set.text: After a serious lung infection last winter, Helen Park spent six weeks in the hospital. The illness was debilitating; at first she could not walk to the bathroom without help, and she felt frail, as if a strong wind could knock her over. Her doctor explained that recovery would be incremental. Day one: stand for two minutes. Day five: walk to the end of the hall. Before getting sick, Helen had a sedentary job, sitting at a computer for nine hours a day, and she admits she rarely exercised. Now walking became her main task. After Helen came home, her daughter visited every afternoon, giving Helen's husband a respite from caring for her. The nurses praised Helen's fortitude, since she rarely complained even on painful days. Today she walks three miles each morning and has asked her office for a standing desk.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “incremental” mean?
options: happening in small steps over time
qs.why: The doctor's plan goes from standing two minutes to walking down the hall: small steps, one after another. “Sudden and complete” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “respite” mean?
options: a short break from something hard
qs.why: The daughter's visits gave Helen's husband a short break from caring for her. It was not a long trip.

qs.q: What change suggests Helen has learned from her illness?
options: She asked for a standing desk so she will sit less at work
She moved closer to the hospital
She asked her daughter to visit every day
qs.why: Before, she sat nine hours a day and rarely exercised; now she walks daily and wants to stand at work. Her daughter's visits happened during recovery and do not show a new habit.

why: Timeline logic: Helen was in hospital, so her husband was not yet caring for her when the daughter's visits gave him a respite; set the visits after she came home.

set.text: When a small painting vanished from the Hartwell Gallery, Detective Ines Moreau was handed one clue: a cryptic note left on the empty wall. It read only, 'The heron flies at six.' From the note she could infer that something would happen at six o'clock on the Heron, a ferry that left the harbor at that hour. But she suspected a ploy. Why would a thief leave directions? While other officers rushed to the ferry, Ines checked camera footage from a nearby parking garage and learned that a guard had been holding clandestine meetings there with an art dealer. She found the painting in the dealer's car at the airport. Prosecutors now allege that the guard switched off the cameras while the dealer, his accomplice, carried the painting out. Both men say they are innocent, and a trial is planned for the spring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “infer” mean?
qs.why: Nobody told Ines about the ferry; she worked it out from the note. “Be told directly” is the opposite of inferring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “allege” mean?
options: say they did wrong without having proved it yet
qs.why: The men say they are innocent and the trial has not happened, so the claim is not yet proved. “Prove” goes too far.

qs.q: Why did Ines doubt the note?
options: The writing was not in English
The ferry left at seven o'clock
A guard told her it was fake
It seemed strange that a thief would leave directions to where he would be
It was signed by the art dealer
She could not understand it at all
qs.why: She asked herself, “Why would a thief leave directions?” She did understand the note; she simply did not trust it.

why: Illogical clue: gallery records would not show meetings held in a parking garage; Ines now finds them on the garage's camera footage.

set.text: Many of us grew up hearing a warning: crack your knuckles and you will get arthritis. It is a widespread misconception, and it is easy to see why people believe it. The popping sound is loud, and it seems as if something must be breaking. But the claim is erroneous. The sound comes from gas bubbles in the fluid inside the joint, not from bones grinding. Researchers have tried to refute the myth in several ways. One doctor cracked the knuckles of only one hand for about sixty years and found no arthritis in either hand. Larger studies comparing knuckle-crackers with non-crackers also found no link. Still, old beliefs are hard to change. When a reader sent us a long rebuttal to an earlier column, pointing to his aunt's sore fingers, we replied with a lucid explanation of the science. We hope this column helps dispel the fear for good.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “erroneous” mean?
options: wrong because it is based on a mistake
qs.why: The column says the claim is false and explains the real cause of the sound. “Partly true” is a near-miss; the column says there is no link at all.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rebuttal” mean?
options: a letter agreeing with the column
an argument trying to show the column was wrong
qs.why: The reader used his aunt's sore fingers to argue against the column. Agreeing with it is the opposite.

qs.q: Why, according to the writer, do so many people believe the myth?
options: Doctors still recommend not cracking knuckles
The loud pop makes it seem as if damage is happening
Gas bubbles slowly wear down bones
qs.why: The writer says the loud sound makes it seem something is breaking. The studies mentioned found no link.

why: Fact precision: the fluid (synovial fluid) is inside the joint capsule, not 'around the joint'.

set.text: For the engineering students at Halden Technical College, last Thursday was a momentous day. After four years of work, they were ready to unveil the satellite they had built. It is small, about the size of a loaf of bread, but building it was a colossal task. The team faced one major constraint: their budget was a tiny fraction of what space companies spend. That forced ingenuity. Instead of buying costly parts, they built the frame from recycled aluminum, used a modified phone camera, and wrote all the control software themselves. Before any launch, a satellite must pass a shaking test that copies the strong vibrations of a rocket ride. Passing it is a prerequisite for a place on the rocket. The students' satellite passed on the first try. If all goes well, it will launch next spring and take photographs of forests to track changes in tree cover.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “constraint” mean?
options: something that limited what they could do
qs.why: Their small budget limited what they could buy. It was not their goal.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prerequisite” mean?
options: something that must happen before something else can
qs.why: The satellite must pass the shaking test before it can get a place on the rocket. It is required, not optional.

qs.q: What forced the students to be so creative?
qs.why: The passage says the small budget “forced ingenuity,” so they reused materials and built parts themselves. The shaking test is a later step, which they passed on the first try.

why: 'why' for the idea question said they passed the shaking test 'easily'; the passage only says on the first try.
